steps.body: Smoke at 275°F for 1 to 1.5 hours, until the peppers are tender and the cheese is melted and golden.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 10 minutes before serving so the filling sets up.

proTips: Stand the peppers in a muffin tin or crimped foil rings so they don't tip over on the grate.
Don't carve the faces too deep or too big — thin walls collapse in the heat.
Use ground beef instead of sausage if you like — Kelly makes it with beef.

title: Bacon Mummy Jalapeño Poppers
summary: Jalapeño poppers wrapped in bacon like mummy bandages, with googly candy eyes. The Halloween appetizer that disappears first.
story: Every Halloween spread needs something the kids can grab with one hand. Cream cheese and cheddar stuffed into jalapeños, wrapped up in bacon strips like little mummies, and smoked low until the bacon crisps. The candy eyes go on after — that's what makes the whole tray look alive.

steps.title: Prep the peppers
steps.body: Cut the jalapeños in half lengthwise and scoop out the seeds and membranes. Wear gloves — your hands will thank you.

steps.title: Mix the filling
steps.body: Stir the cream cheese, cheddar, and garlic powder together until smooth.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.body: Fill each jalapeño half generously with the cheese mixture.

steps.title: Wrap like a mummy
steps.body: Wrap each popper with a strip of bacon, crisscrossing it like mummy bandages. Leave a little gap near the top for the face.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F for 1.5 to 2 hours, until the bacon is crisped and the cheese is bubbly.

steps.title: Add the eyes
steps.body: Let them cool a couple minutes, then press two candy eyes into the cheese in the face gap of each mummy.

proTips: Thin bacon crisps better than thick cut — thick bacon stays chewy at 250°F.
Put the eyes on after the smoke, not before. They melt into blobs in the heat.

title: Smoked Pumpkin Pie
wood: Apple or pecan (light — easy on the smoke)
summary: Classic pumpkin pie baked on the smoker with a whisper of apple or pecan smoke. Fall in a crust.
story: The smoker isn't just for meat — it bakes a fine pie. Same pumpkin pie you grew up with, but the crust picks up the faintest kiss of apple or pecan smoke on its way through. Keep the smoke light; this one is about the pie, not the pit.

steps.title: Heat the smoker
steps.body: Get the smoker to 350°F, indirect, with a light wood like apple or pecan. Go easy — a little smoke goes a long way on dessert.

steps.title: Mix the filling
steps.body: Whisk the pumpkin, evaporated milk, eggs, brown sugar, pumpkin pie spice, and salt until completely smooth.

steps.title: Fill the crust
steps.body: Pour the filling into the pie crust.

steps.title: Smoke-bake
steps.body: Bake on the smoker at 350°F for 50 to 60 minutes, until the edges are set and the center barely jiggles when you nudge the pan.

steps.title: Cool
steps.body: Cool at least 2 hours so the filling sets. Serve with whipped cream.

proTips: Light wood and a clean fire — heavy smoke turns the pie bitter.
That little jiggle in the center is right. It sets as it cools; an overbaked pie cracks.

title: Bacon Mummy Meatloaf
summary: Meatloaf wrapped in a bacon lattice like a mummy, with olive eyes. Smoked low and slow.
story: The kids will not stop staring at this one — and then they'll eat half of it. A solid backyard meatloaf wrapped in a woven bacon lattice like mummy bandages, smoked until the bacon crisps and the middle hits temp. The olive eyes go on at the end. Carve it at the table for maximum effect.

items: 1/4 cup ketchup or BBQ sauce, for glazing

steps.title: Mix the loaf
steps.body: Mix the beef, breadcrumbs, eggs, onion, garlic, ketchup, Worcestershire, rub, salt, and pepper until just combined. Don't overwork it. Shape into a loaf on a foil-lined sheet pan or a grill-safe pan.

steps.title: Weave the mummy
steps.body: Lay out the bacon in a lattice over the loaf, crisscrossing like mummy bandages. Leave a small gap near one end for the face.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 275°F for 2.5 to 3 hours, until the internal temp hits 160°F. Brush with ketchup or BBQ sauce in the last 30 minutes.

steps.title: Eyes and rest
steps.body: Rest 15 minutes, then press two black olive halves into the face gap for eyes. Slice and serve.

proTips: Thin bacon crisps; thick bacon stays chewy. Go thin.
Put the loaf on a wire rack over a sheet pan so the bottom doesn't steam.

title: Smoked Bat Wings
summary: Chicken wings in a dark, sticky sweet-heat glaze. They come out looking like they flew straight out of a cave.
story: The dark rub and the sticky glaze do all the Halloween work here — these wings come off the pit almost black and shining. Sweet heat underneath, crispy-edged, gone in minutes. Make more than you think you need.

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Pat the wings dry. Toss with all the rub ingredients until evenly coated.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F for about 1.5 hours, until the wings hit 175°F internal and the skin has tightened up.

steps.title: Glaze
steps.body: Warm the BBQ sauce, honey, and soy sauce together. Toss the wings in the glaze.

steps.title: Set the glaze
steps.body: Return to the smoker for 15 minutes so the glaze sets sticky and dark. Serve hot.

proTips: Dry wings = crispier skin. Pat them down and let them air-dry in the fridge an hour if you can.
Don't glaze too early or the sugars burn. Glaze at the end.

title: Pulled Pork Stuffed Mini Pumpkins
summary: Little pie pumpkins stuffed with pulled pork and cheddar, smoked until the pumpkin goes tender.
story: This is what you do with leftover pulled pork in October. Hollow out little pie pumpkins, pack them with pork and cheese, and let the smoker do the rest. The pumpkin steams itself tender from the inside and you can scoop it right out with the pork.

steps.title: Hollow the pumpkins
steps.body: Cut the tops off the pumpkins and scoop out the seeds and stringy guts. Sprinkle the insides lightly with salt and pepper.

steps.title: Fill
steps.body: Toss the pulled pork with the BBQ sauce, onion, and half the cheddar. Pack the mixture into the pumpkins and top with the rest of the cheddar. Set the tops back on, tilted like little hats.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 275°F for about 1 hour, until the pumpkin flesh is tender when poked and the cheese is melted.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Serve whole — scoop the tender pumpkin right out with the pork.

proTips: Use pie pumpkins, not carving pumpkins — carving pumpkins are stringy and bland.
Any leftover smoked meat works here: brisket, chicken, turkey.

title: Smoked Hot Apple Cider
summary: A pot of spiced apple cider warmed on the smoker with a whisper of apple wood smoke.
story: While the Halloween cook runs, a pot of cider rides along on the smoker and picks up the faintest kiss of apple wood. Cinnamon, cloves, star anise, orange — the whole house smells like October. Ladle it hot straight from the pot.

steps.title: Load the pot
steps.body: Pour the cider into a cast iron Dutch oven or heavy pot. Stir in the brown sugar if using, then add the cinnamon sticks, cloves, star anise, and orange slices.

steps.title: Smoke-warm
steps.body: Set the pot on the smoker at 275°F with light apple wood for 1.5 to 2 hours, stirring once or twice, until steaming hot and spiced through.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Ladle into mugs, straining out the whole spices if you like. Keep the pot on the warm side of the pit for refills.

proTips: Light smoke only — heavy smoke turns cider bitter. Apple wood, small fire.
Tie the cloves and star anise in cheesecloth for easy fishing out.

title: Halloween Snack Mix
summary: Bold-style Chex snack mix toasted on the smoker, then tossed with candy corn and chocolate candies.
story: This one's the Bold version — extra Worcestershire, garlic, and onion, with bagel chips folded in like the real Bold blend. An hour on the smoker, then it cools down and gets the Halloween treatment with candy corn and chocolate candies. The bowl empties itself.

items: 1 cup orange and black chocolate candies

steps.title: Coat
steps.body: Toss the Chex, pretzels, bagel chips, and peanuts in a big foil pan. Drizzle with the melted butter, Worcestershire, seasoned salt, garlic powder, and onion powder; toss to coat.

steps.title: Smoke-toast
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F for 1 hour, stirring every 15 minutes, until crisp and toasted.

steps.title: Cool and candy
steps.body: Cool completely — the candy melts if the mix is warm — then fold in the candy corn and chocolate candies.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Bowl it up. Keeps a week in an airtight container, if it survives the night.

proTips: Stir every 15 minutes or the bottom pieces over-toast.
Wait until it's fully cool before the candy goes in — warm mix makes a melted mess.

title: Skillet Fried Apples
summary: Apple slices fried in a cast iron skillet with butter, brown sugar, and cinnamon until tender and glazed.
story: Kristy's request. Sliced apples cooked down in butter and brown sugar with cinnamon and nutmeg until they're tender and swimming in syrup. Serve them next to pork chops like they do down South, or over a scoop of vanilla ice cream. Either way, don't expect leftovers.

items: 5 firm apples (Golden Delicious or Granny Smith), cored and sliced

steps.title: Melt the butter
steps.body: Melt the butter in a cast iron skillet over medium heat.

steps.title: Add everything
steps.body: Add the apple slices, brown sugar, cinnamon, nutmeg, salt, and the splash of apple juice. Stir to coat.

steps.title: Fry
steps.body: Cook 15 to 20 minutes, stirring now and then, until the apples are tender and glazed in a thick syrup.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Serve warm — next to pork, or over ice cream.

proTips: Firm apples hold their shape; soft ones turn to mush. Golden Delicious or Granny Smith.
Don't walk away at the end — the sugar syrup can go from glazed to scorched fast.

title: Candy Apple BBQ Chicken
finish: 175°F in the thigh, 160-165°F in the breast, glaze set sticky
summary: Smoked chicken halves under a sticky apple butter glaze that sets up like a candy apple. Sweet, smoky, and shining.
story: Inspired by Lane's BBQ's candy apple chicken halves — this is our own take with Ember House Rub and a warm apple butter glaze that caramelizes right on the bird. The glaze goes on late so the sugars shine instead of burn. Cut into halves, they look like something off a Halloween candy table and eat like the best BBQ chicken you've had.

items: 2 whole chickens (3-4 lbs each), cut in half — or 4 store-bought chicken halves

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Pat the halves dry. Season all over with Ember House Rub, working some under the breast skin. Rest 30 minutes.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 275°F over apple or cherry wood, skin-side up, until the breast reads 150°F — about 2 to 2 1/2 hours.

steps.title: Make the glaze
steps.body: Warm the apple butter, honey, apple juice, and butter in a saucepan until melted together into a smooth glaze.

steps.title: Glaze and set
steps.body: Brush the glaze thick over every half. Return to the smoker for 15 minutes so it sets.

steps.title: Finish candy-style
steps.body: Brush with Ember Finishing Glaze and give it 10 more minutes until sticky and caramelized. Thighs should read 175°F, breast 160-165°F. Rest 10 minutes and serve with extra glaze on the side.

proTips: Glaze late — the sugars in the apple butter and honey will burn if they go on too early.
Warm glaze brushes on smoother and sticks better than cold glaze straight from the jar.
Don't skip the rest. Ten minutes lets the glaze firm up into that candy shine.

title: Armadillo Eggs
summary: Jalapeños stuffed with cream cheese, wrapped in sausage and bacon, smoked until crisp. The ultimate pop-in-your-mouth BBQ bite.
story: Part jalapeño popper, part scotch egg, all barbecue. The sausage shell keeps the cheese from escaping and the bacon bastes the whole thing as it crisps. One cut open with the cheese running out will end the argument about who gets the last one.

steps.title: Prep the peppers
steps.body: Cut the tops off the jalapeños, halve lengthwise, and scrape out the seeds and membranes. Leave some membrane if you like heat. Wear gloves.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.body: Mix the cream cheese, cheddar, and 1 Tbsp Ember House Rub. Stuff each jalapeño half full.

steps.title: Wrap in sausage
steps.body: Divide the sausage into 12 portions. Flatten each into a thin patty and wrap it completely around a stuffed half, pinching the seams shut.

steps.title: Wrap in bacon
steps.body: Dust with the rest of the rub, then wrap each one in a slice of bacon. Secure with a toothpick.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 275°F about 2 hours, until the bacon is crisp and the sausage reads 160°F inside. Brush with Ember Finishing Glaze in the last 15 minutes if you want them sticky.

proTips: Thin bacon beats thick here — it actually crisps instead of staying chewy.
Pinch the sausage seams shut or the cheese will find its way out.
Make a double batch. They vanish.

title: Molasses Pull Taffy
finish: Hard ball stage, light tan and satiny after pulling
summary: Old-time mountain taffy pull candy — dark molasses, chewy, wrapped in wax paper twists.
story: Taffy pulls were a social event in the mountains — everybody's hands got buttered and everybody got candy. Molasses is the Appalachian sweetener, and pulled slow it turns light and satiny. This isn't barbecue, but it belongs to the same people.

items: 2 Tbsp butter, plus more for your hands

steps.title: Cook
steps.body: Combine everything except the baking soda in a heavy pot. Cook over medium heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then stop stirring. Cook to 260°F (hard ball stage).

steps.title: Foam and pour
steps.body: Stir in the baking soda — it will foam up. Pour onto a buttered slab or sheet pan.

steps.title: Cool
steps.body: Cool 10-15 minutes until you can handle it without burning yourself.

steps.title: Pull
steps.body: Butter your hands. Stretch, fold, and stretch again for 15-20 minutes until the taffy turns light tan and satiny.

steps.title: Cut and wrap
steps.body: Pull into ropes, cut with buttered scissors, and wrap each piece in wax paper twists.

proTips: A second pair of hands makes the pulling go twice as fast — that's how the old taffy pulls worked.
If it sticks to your teeth, you pulled it right.
Wrap every piece — left unwrapped, they'll melt into one big lump.

title: Black Walnut Fudge
finish: Soft ball stage, thick and matte after beating
summary: Classic chocolate fudge loaded with black walnuts — the Appalachian nut.
story: Black walnuts aren't like the English walnuts in the store — they're stronger, earthier, and they taste like the mountains. Folks used to gather them in the fall and crack them on a rock. Folded into fudge, they're the whole reason for the recipe.

steps.title: Cook
steps.body: Combine the sugar, cocoa, milk, and salt in a heavy pot. Cook over medium heat, stirring until dissolved, then stop stirring. Cook to 234°F (soft ball stage).

steps.title: Cool
steps.body: Remove from heat and drop in the butter — don't stir. Let it cool to 110°F (lukewarm to the touch).

steps.title: Beat
steps.body: Add the vanilla and beat with a wooden spoon until thick and it loses its gloss.

steps.title: Nuts and pan
steps.body: Fold in the black walnuts. Spread in a buttered 8x8 pan. Cool completely, then cut into squares.

proTips: Black walnuts are stronger than English walnuts — a cup is plenty.
Don't beat it before it cools to lukewarm or it will go grainy.
A candy thermometer is worth it here — 5 degrees off either way changes the texture.

title: Sorghum Peanut Brittle
finish: Hard crack stage, thin and glassy
summary: Peanut brittle made with Kentucky sorghum instead of corn syrup — deeper, darker, better.
story: Sorghum was the mountain sweetener — folks grew the cane and cooked the syrup down every fall. Swapping it for corn syrup in peanut brittle gives you a deeper, almost smoky sweetness. Use cocktail or Spanish peanuts — raw ones are hard to find, and these go in late so they don't scorch.

items: 1 1/2 cups cocktail peanuts or Spanish peanuts
1/4 tsp salt (skip if your peanuts are salted)

steps.title: Cook the syrup
steps.body: Combine the sugar, sorghum, and water in a heavy pot. Cook over medium heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves, to 290°F.

steps.title: Add peanuts
steps.body: Stir in the peanuts and cook to 300°F (hard crack stage), stirring so nothing scorches.

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: Off the heat, stir in the butter, then the baking soda and vanilla — it will foam up.

steps.title: Spread and break
steps.body: Pour onto a buttered sheet pan and spread thin. Cool completely, then break into pieces.

proTips: Have everything measured before you start — once it hits temp it moves fast.
Thin spreads snap better than thick ones.
Cocktail or Spanish peanuts go in late because they're already roasted — raw peanuts would go in much earlier.

title: Peanut Butter Potato Candy
summary: Depression-era Appalachian candy — mashed potato, powdered sugar, and peanut butter rolled into pinwheels.
story: Sounds strange until you taste it. This came out of hard times in the mountains — a potato, a bag of powdered sugar, and peanut butter turned into candy. Kelly's had it, and it eats like a peanut butter roll.

items: 1/2 cup plain mashed potato (no butter, no salt — just potato)
1 lb powdered sugar (about 4 cups), plus more for dusting

steps.title: Make the dough
steps.body: Mash the warm potato completely smooth — no lumps. Stir in the vanilla, then beat in the powdered sugar a cup at a time until it forms a stiff dough.

steps.title: Roll out
steps.body: Roll the dough on a powdered-sugar-dusted surface into a rectangle about 1/4 inch thick.

steps.title: Fill
steps.body: Spread peanut butter over the whole thing, edge to edge.

steps.title: Roll and chill
steps.body: Roll it up jelly-roll style, wrap in plastic, and chill at least an hour. Slice into pinwheels.

proTips: The dough is sticky — that's normal, just keep dusting with powdered sugar.
Chill before slicing or the pinwheels squish.
The potato must be lump-free — push it through a ricer or sieve if you have to.

title: Blackberry Jam Cake
summary: Kentucky tradition — spice cake with blackberry jam baked right in, frosted all over with caramel icing.
story: The jam goes in the batter, not between the layers — that's the Kentucky way Kelly knows. It bakes into the crumb and keeps the cake moist for days. Frost the whole thing with caramel icing and don't stop at one slice.

items: 1 cup blackberry jam (seedless if you can find it)
1 cup chopped pecans or black walnuts (optional)

steps.title: Make the batter
steps.body: Cream the butter and sugar until fluffy. Beat in the eggs one at a time, then beat in the blackberry jam — it goes right in the batter.

steps.title: Combine
steps.body: Whisk the flour, baking soda, and spices. Add to the batter alternating with the buttermilk. Fold in the nuts if using.

steps.title: Bake
steps.body: Pour into three greased 9-inch pans (or one 9x13). Bake at 350°F for 25-30 minutes, until a toothpick comes out clean. Cool completely.

steps.title: Caramel icing
steps.body: Melt the butter, stir in the brown sugar and milk, and boil 2 minutes. Cool slightly, then beat in the powdered sugar and vanilla.

steps.title: Frost
steps.body: Stack the layers and frost the whole cake all over with the caramel icing.

proTips: The jam is the flavor — use a good one, or homemade if you've got it.
The cake gets better the next day as the jam settles into the crumb.
Work fast with the caramel icing — it sets up as it cools.

title: Cowboy Beans
summary: Ground beef, bacon, and three kinds of beans in a sweet-smoky sauce. Made for the smoker.
story: Every cookout needs a pot of these. Beef, bacon, and beans go in the Dutch oven, the smoker does the rest, and the pot comes back empty.

steps.title: Brown the meat
steps.body: Brown the ground beef with the bacon, onion, and bell pepper in a cast-iron skillet or Dutch oven. Drain the grease.

steps.title: Mix it up
steps.body: Stir in everything else.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 275°F for 2 hours uncovered, stirring once halfway, until thick and bubbly. (Oven works too — 350°F for 1 hour.)

proTips: Don't skip draining the canned beans or it goes soupy.
Leftovers are even better the next day.

title: Old-Fashioned Popcorn Balls
summary: Crunchy, buttery, and just sticky enough. Tint them orange for the Halloween table.
story: Every fall needs a batch of these. Hot syrup, buttered hands, and popcorn — shaped fast before it sets.

items: 10 cups popped popcorn (about 1/2 cup kernels), unpopped kernels picked out
1 Tbsp butter, plus more for your hands

steps.title: Prep
steps.body: Put the popcorn in a big buttered bowl.

steps.title: Cook the syrup
steps.body: In a saucepan, stir the sugar, corn syrup, water, butter, and salt. Boil until it hits 250°F on a candy thermometer (hard-ball stage), about 5 minutes. Stir in the vanilla and food coloring if using.

steps.title: Coat
steps.body: Pour over the popcorn and toss fast to coat.

steps.title: Shape
steps.body: Butter your hands and shape into balls about the size of a tennis ball. Work quick — it sets fast.

steps.title: Cool
steps.body: Cool on wax paper.

proTips: Don't skip the butter on your hands or you'll be picking popcorn off your palms.
If the syrup gets too cool to shape, warm it 10 seconds in the microwave.

title: Smoke & Ember Turkey Brine
summary: The night-before soak that keeps the bird juicy through a long smoke. Salt, brown sugar, citrus, and herbs.
story: A dry turkey ruins Thanksgiving. This brine is the insurance policy — salt and sugar carry the citrus and herbs deep into the meat overnight, so the bird stays juicy no matter how long the smoke runs.

items: 1 whole garlic bulb, cut in half crosswise

steps.title: Dissolve
steps.body: In a big stockpot, heat 1/2 gallon of the water with the salt, brown sugar, peppercorns, and bay leaves. Stir until the salt and sugar dissolve, then pull it off the heat.

steps.title: Cool it down
steps.body: Add the remaining 1 1/2 gallons of cold water, the garlic, oranges, onion, thyme, and rosemary. Let it cool completely — cold to the touch, not warm.

steps.title: Submerge the bird
steps.body: Lower the turkey into the brine breast-side down. It needs to stay fully submerged — weigh it down with a plate if it floats.

steps.title: Wait
steps.body: Refrigerate 12 to 24 hours. Don't go past 24 or the meat gets hammy.

steps.title: Rinse and dry
steps.body: Pull the bird out, rinse it under cold water, and pat it completely dry with paper towels. Let it sit uncovered in the fridge for an hour so the skin dries — that's what gets you crispy skin on the smoker.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Season and smoke like normal. Skip any extra salt in your rub — the brine already handled it.

proTips: No fridge space? A brining bag in a cooler full of ice works — just keep it under 40°F.
This fits a 12 to 16 pound bird. Bigger than that, make half again as much brine.
Don't use table salt here. The iodine makes the brine taste tinny.

title: Pitmaster's Mop Sauce
summary: The thin baste that keeps long smokes juicy and builds bark. Mop it on, don't pour it.
story: The mop is the pitmaster's paintbrush. This thin vinegar mop goes on every 45 minutes once the bark sets — it keeps the meat from drying out and lays down layer after layer of flavor without washing anything off.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body: Whisk everything together in a saucepan. Bring it just to a simmer over medium heat, stirring until the sugar and salt dissolve.

steps.title: Cool & bottle
steps.body: Pull it off the heat and let it cool. Pour it into a squeeze bottle or a bowl — whatever you're mopping from.

steps.title: Mop
steps.body: Mop the meat every 45 minutes to an hour during the cook, starting after the first 2 hours. Thin coat — you're basting, not drowning it.

steps.title: Keep it warm
steps.body: Keep the mop warm on the pit or the stove while you cook. Cold mop on hot meat is a bark killer.

proTips: Don't mop in the first 2 hours. Let the bark set first or you'll wash it right off.
Built for pork butt, ribs, and brisket — anything with a long cook.
Leftover mop keeps a week in the fridge. Don't save what touched raw meat — make fresh.

title: Citrus Mojo Smoked Pork Shoulder
summary: Florida's answer to pulled pork — bright citrus, heavy garlic, Cuban soul.
story: This is what happens when a pork shoulder spends the night in citrus and garlic and then meets oak smoke. The mojo injection carries orange, lime, and garlic deep into the meat, and the long smoke turns it into the juiciest pulled pork you'll ever make.

steps.title: Mix the mojo
steps.body: Whisk the mojo together. Warm it slightly — not hot, just warm to the touch.

steps.title: Inject
steps.body: Inject the pork shoulder in a grid pattern, about an inch apart. Use all of it — this is a big piece of meat and it drinks it up.

steps.title: Rub & rest
steps.body: Coat the outside with the rub. Wrap it tight and refrigerate overnight, 8 to 12 hours.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F over oak or citrus wood until it probes tender, 200–205°F. Plan on 1.5 to 2 hours per pound.

steps.title: Rest & pull
steps.body: Rest it wrapped in a cooler for at least an hour. Pull it and spoon some of the drippings back over the meat.

proTips: Fresh citrus only — the bottled stuff tastes like cleaning product in the smoker.
This one's built for an 8 to 10 pound Boston butt.
Leftover mojo (that never touched raw meat) makes a killer dipping sauce.

title: Florida Smoked Fish Dip
summary: The dockside classic. Smoky, creamy, with a little kick — built for crackers and cold drinks.
story: Every dock in Florida has a version of this. Smoke the fish low, flake it chunky, fold it into cream cheese with lemon and heat, and let it sit overnight. By the next day it's the best thing on the table.

items: 1 lb smoked white fish (mahi, kingfish, or amberjack), flaked

steps.title: Smoke the fish
steps.body: Smoke the fish at 225°F over a mild wood (alder or apple) until it flakes easily, about 1 to 1.5 hours. Let it cool.

steps.title: Flake
steps.body: Flake the fish into a bowl, picking out any bones. Don't shred it to mush — you want some chunks in there.

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Fold in the cream cheese, mayo, sour cream, lemon juice, and hot sauce. Stir until it's combined but still chunky.

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Fold in the green onions, parsley, Old Bay, pepper, and garlic powder.

steps.title: Chill
steps.body: Cover and refrigerate at least 2 hours — overnight is better. The flavors need time to get to know each other.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Serve cold with crackers, celery, or thick-cut potato chips.

proTips: Oily fish works best — kingfish and mahi are the Florida classics, but mullet is the old-school pick.
If your fish comes out too dry from the smoker, add an extra spoonful of mayo. Nobody will know.
This keeps 4 to 5 days in the fridge. It won't last that long.

title: Key West Smoked Shrimp
summary: Pink shrimp, citrus butter, and a kiss of smoke. Done in under an hour.
story: Key West pink shrimp barely need anything — a little citrus butter, a little garlic, and a whisper of mild smoke. They cook fast, so don't walk away. Thirty minutes in the smoker and they're the best thing at the table.

items: 2 lbs large Key West pink shrimp (or Gulf shrimp), peeled and deveined, tails on
Lime wedges and fresh parsley, for serving

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Toss the shrimp with the melted butter, lime juice, garlic, Old Bay, pepper, and smoked paprika. Let it sit 15 minutes — no longer, or the lime starts cooking the shrimp.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Get the smoker to 225°F. Mild wood — alder or apple. Hickory will bully the shrimp. Lay the shrimp out on a grill pan or frog mat in a single layer.

steps.title: Cook fast
steps.body: Smoke for 30 to 45 minutes, until they're pink, firm, and curled.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Squeeze fresh lime over the top, scatter the parsley, and serve hot. Cocktail sauce optional — these don't need it.

proTips: Don't overcook them. Shrimp go from perfect to rubber in about five minutes — start checking at 30.
If you can't find Key West pinks, any Gulf shrimp works. Just don't use the tiny salad shrimp.
These are dangerous as an appetizer because nobody saves room for dinner.

title: Key West Key Lime Pie
summary: The real thing: creamy yellow, never green. Tart, sweet, and simple the way the Keys made it.
story: I've made this pie, and I'm telling you — the real Key West version is almost insultingly simple. Condensed milk, egg yolks, Key lime juice, graham cracker crust. No green food coloring, no shortcuts on the limes. The acid does all the work.

items: 1/2 cup Key lime juice (fresh Key limes, or Nellie & Joe's bottled)

steps.title: Crust
steps.body: Heat the oven to 350°F. Mix the graham cracker crumbs, sugar, and melted butter. Press it firm into a 9-inch pie dish, bottom and sides. Bake 10 minutes, then let it cool.

steps.title: Filling
steps.body: Whisk the egg yolks and condensed milk until smooth. Slowly whisk in the Key lime juice — it'll thicken up on its own. That's the magic.

steps.title: Bake
steps.body: Pour it into the cooled crust. Bake 15 minutes, until the center is just set with a slight jiggle.

steps.title: Chill
steps.body: Cool it on the counter, then refrigerate at least 3 hours — overnight is better.

steps.title: Top & serve
steps.body: Top with whipped cream and lime slices right before serving.

proTips: Real Key lime pie is yellow, not green. If it's green, something's wrong.
Don't use regular limes — Key limes or the bottled Key lime juice. Big Persian limes taste flat in this.
Sweetened condensed milk, never regular milk. That's the whole trick the sponge divers figured out.

title: Apple Pie Stuffed Pork Loin
summary: A butterflied pork loin stuffed with apple pie filling, wrapped in sweet-savory rub and finished with apple glaze.
story: Sweet meets savory in the best way. The pork loin gets butterflied, loaded with apple pie filling, rolled tight, and smoked until the glaze caramelizes on the outside. Slice it into pinwheels and watch them disappear.

steps.title: Butterfly
steps.body: Butterfly the pork loin — cut it open like a book so it lays flat, about 3/4 inch thick. Don't cut all the way through.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.body: Spread the apple pie filling down the center, leaving a 1-inch border on all sides.

steps.title: Roll & tie
steps.body: Roll it up tight from one long side and tie it with butcher's twine every 2 inches so nothing escapes.

steps.title: Rub
steps.body: Coat the whole outside with the rub. Every inch of it.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F over apple or cherry wood until it hits 145°F internal, about 2.5 to 3 hours.

steps.title: Glaze
steps.body: While it smokes, simmer the glaze ingredients until thick enough to coat a spoon, about 10 minutes. Brush it on during the last 30 minutes.

steps.title: Rest & slice
steps.body: Rest 15 minutes before slicing into pinwheels.

proTips: Tie it tight. Apple pie filling wants to escape — the twine is the only thing standing between you and a mess.
Don't skip the rest. Cut it too soon and the filling runs everywhere.
Feeds 8 to 10 off a 5-pounder.

title: Sweet Apple Glaze
summary: Apple juice, brown sugar, and cinnamon reduced into a sticky-sweet glaze. Made for pork.
story: This started as the finishing glaze for the apple pie stuffed loin, but it's too good to keep locked to one recipe. Brush it on pork chops, ribs, chicken — anything that wants a sweet apple shine.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body: Combine everything in a saucepan over medium heat. Stir until the sugar dissolves.

steps.title: Reduce
steps.body: Simmer 10 minutes, stirring now and then, until it thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon.

steps.title: Use
steps.body: Brush onto pork or poultry during the last 30 minutes of the cook. Keeps 2 weeks in the fridge.

proTips: Don't walk away — sugar burns fast once it starts thickening.
Warm it before brushing. Cold glaze seizes on hot meat.

title: Traditional Stuffed Pork Loin
summary: Peppers, onions, Italian sausage, and melted cheese rolled into a pork loin. The classic.
story: This is the stuffed loin I grew up on — savory all the way. Italian sausage, peppers, and onions with a core of melted cheese, rolled into a pork loin and smoked until the outside crisps and the inside goes molten.

steps.title: Cook the stuffing
steps.body: Brown the Italian sausage in a skillet, breaking it up. Add the onion, peppers, and garlic — cook until soft, about 8 minutes. Let it cool slightly.

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Mix in the mozzarella, Parmesan, parsley, and Italian seasoning.

steps.title: Butterfly
steps.body: Butterfly the pork loin — cut it open like a book so it lays flat, about 3/4 inch thick.

steps.title: Stuff & roll
steps.body: Spread the stuffing down the center, leaving a 1-inch border. Roll it up tight and tie with butcher's twine every 2 inches.

steps.title: Rub
steps.body: Coat the outside with the rub.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F over hickory or oak until it hits 145°F internal, about 2.5 to 3 hours.

steps.title: Rest & slice
steps.body: Rest 15 minutes before slicing into pinwheels.

proTips: Don't overstuff it — if the filling's spilling out before you tie it, you've got too much.
Great the next day sliced thin for sandwiches.

title: Chimichurri
summary: Bright, garlicky, and built for anything that came off the fire.
story: Chimichurri is Argentina's answer to steak sauce, and it embarrasses the bottled stuff. Parsley, oregano, garlic, and red pepper flakes swimming in good olive oil — chop it by hand, let it sit, and spoon it over everything.

items: 1/4 cup fresh oregano leaves, finely chopped (or 2 Tbsp dried)

steps.title: Chop
steps.body: Chop everything by hand — don't food-process it into baby food. You want texture.

steps.title: Mix & rest
steps.body: Stir it all together in a bowl. Let it sit at room temperature for at least 30 minutes so the flavors marry.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Spoon it over sliced brisket, tri-tip, chicken, or anything grilled.

proTips: Keeps a week in the fridge. The oil will solidify — let it come back to room temp before serving.
More heat? Double the red pepper flakes. Less? Leave them out entirely.

title: Smoked Spam Burnt Ends
summary: Cubed, rubbed sweet with Smoke & Ember rub, smoked, and glazed with Smoke & Ember sauce. Poor man's burnt ends that eat like candy.
story: Don't sleep on Spam. Cube it, hit it with Smoke & Ember Sweet Rub, and smoke it until the edges caramelize — then drown it in Smoke & Ember BBQ Sauce glaze and give it one more ride. These eat like meat candy.

items: 2 cans (12 oz each) Spam, cut into 1-inch cubes

steps.title: Cube & rub
steps.body: Cut the Spam into 1-inch cubes. Toss them in mustard as a binder if you want — helps the rub stick. Coat every cube generously with Smoke & Ember Sweet Rub.

steps.title: First smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F over hickory or apple for 2 hours, until the edges start to crisp and caramelize.

steps.title: Glaze & pan
steps.body: Toss the cubes in the Smoke & Ember BBQ Sauce glaze. Put them in a foil pan, cover with foil, and back on the smoker for 1 more hour.

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: Uncover and give them 15 more minutes so the glaze gets sticky and tacky.

proTips: Don't skip the second smoke in the pan — that's where they go from good to candy.
Two cans sounds like a lot until they're gone in ten minutes.

title: Smoked Frog Legs
summary: Brined, smoked, then flash-fried. Crispy outside, tender inside — tastes like the bayou.
story: Frog legs done right are something special. A buttermilk brine pulls out any gaminess, a kiss of pecan smoke lays down flavor, and a hot fry finishes them crispy. If you've never had them — they taste like a cross between chicken and fish.

items: 2 lbs frog legs (hind legs only), thawed if frozen

steps.title: Brine
steps.body: Soak the frog legs in the buttermilk, hot sauce, and salt for at least 2 hours — overnight is better.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Pat them dry (don't rinse). Smoke at 225°F over pecan or oak for 45 minutes. You're laying down smoke, not cooking them through.

steps.title: Dredge
steps.body: Heat oil to 350°F in a cast iron skillet or fryer. Dredge the smoked legs in the flour-cornmeal mix, pressing it on good.

steps.title: Fry
steps.body: Fry 3-4 minutes per side until golden brown and crispy. Drain on a rack, not paper towels — keeps them crispy.

proTips: Don't overcook them. Frog legs go from perfect to rubber in about a minute.
Want to kick it up? Add a little cayenne pepper to the dredge.
Remoulade or comeback sauce for dipping. Hot sauce works too.

title: Pacific Island Pork Butt
summary: Pacific Island flair — smoked pork butt braised in coconut milk, soy, vinegar, and hot peppers until it falls apart.
story: Inspired by Manny, my buddy in Saipan, who told me they cook pork butt with coconut milk over there. I gave it the Smoke & Ember treatment — smoke it first for bark and flavor, then braise it island-style until it shreds. Serve it over rice and don't be shy with the sauce.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Season the pork butt with salt and pepper. Smoke at 250°F for 4 hours — building bark and smoke flavor, not finishing it.

steps.title: Braise
steps.body: Put the butt in a large pot or Dutch oven. Add everything else around it.

steps.title: Low & slow
steps.body: Bring to a simmer, cover, and cook low 3-4 hours, turning the butt once halfway. Done when it shreds with a fork.

steps.title: Soak
steps.body: Pull the pork apart in the pot and let it soak up the sauce for 15 minutes.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Serve over white rice with plenty of the braising liquid spooned on top.

proTips: The vinegar and soy are the backbone — don't skip either one.
Coconut milk goes in for richness.
This makes a lot of sauce. That's the point — it's for the rice.

title: Pacific Island Parrotfish in Coconut Milk
summary: Pacific Island flair — parrotfish (uhu) simmered in coconut milk with onion, tomato, and a little heat.
story: Inspired by Manny, my buddy in Saipan, who gave this one the thumbs up. Island-style parrotfish simmered gentle in coconut milk — the kind of dish that makes you wish you lived closer to the water.

items: 2 lbs parrotfish fillets (uhu), cut into chunks

steps.title: Prep fish
steps.body: Season the fish with salt and pepper. Lightly dust with flour.

steps.title: Brown
steps.body: Brown the fish quickly in hot oil, just a minute per side. Pull it out.

steps.title: Sauce
steps.body: In the same pot, soften the onion and garlic. Add the coconut milk, tomatoes, lemon juice, salt, and hot pepper.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body: Bring to a gentle simmer — don't boil it hard or the coconut milk gets lumpy. Lay the fish back in and simmer 10-12 minutes until it flakes.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Serve over rice with the sauce spooned over everything.

proTips: Don't walk away from coconut milk on high heat. Low and gentle wins.
Any firm white fish works if you can't get parrotfish — but the real thing is worth it.

title: Kentucky Fried Chicken (Copycat)
summary: The 11 herbs and spices, as close as anyone's ever gotten. Deep fry it or grill it — cook's choice.
story: This is the Colonel's recipe as close as it gets outside the vault. White pepper is the secret — that's the back-of-the-throat heat you remember. Deep fry it classic style, or do the grill vortex method with no oil bath.

items: 1 whole chicken (3-4 lbs), cut into 8 pieces
2 cups flour mixed with all the spices above

steps.title: Soak
steps.body: Soak the chicken in buttermilk and beaten egg for 30 minutes.

steps.title: Dredge
steps.body: Mix the flour and all 11 spices. Pull each piece from the buttermilk, dredge in the seasoned flour, and rest on a wire rack for 15 minutes to set the crust.

steps.title: Cook — pick your method
steps.body: DEEP FRY: Fry at 350°F in shortening for 12-18 minutes depending on the piece. GRILL: Pile coals in a vortex (or center), arrange chicken around the edge, lid on at 400-450°F for 30-40 minutes, flipping once. No oil needed.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Drain on a wire rack. 165°F inside. Don't cut into it right away — let it rest 5 minutes.

proTips: The real KFC is pressure-fried — you can't do that at home safely, but this gets you 95% of the way on flavor.
Don't skip the rest before cooking. That's what keeps the breading on.
Shortening over oil for frying — that's the move.

title: Lee's Famous Recipe Chicken (Copycat)
summary: Lighter and crispier than KFC — the Colonel's nephew's recipe, big in Kentucky.
story: Lee's was started by Lee Cummings — Colonel Sanders' own nephew. It's huge in Kentucky but most folks outside the state never heard of it. Lighter, crispier crust than KFC thanks to self-rising flour. The underdog Kentucky chicken, and their loss is your gain.

items: 1 whole chicken (3-4 lbs), cut into 8 pieces
3 cups self-rising flour mixed with 1/4 cup of the spice blend

steps.title: Brine
steps.body: Brine the chicken in buttermilk and salt for at least 4 hours — overnight is better.

steps.title: Dredge
steps.body: Mix the self-rising flour with the spice blend. Pull each piece from the brine, dredge in the seasoned flour, pressing it on. Rest 10 minutes.

steps.title: Fry
steps.body: Fry at 325°F for 12-15 minutes until deep golden and crispy. 165°F inside.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Drain on a wire rack and rest 10 minutes before serving.

proTips: Self-rising flour is non-negotiable — that's what makes the crust light and puffy.
Fry a touch lower than KFC (325°F) so the lighter crust doesn't burn before the chicken cooks through.

title: Cinnamon-Spiced Pork Belly Rolls
summary: Pork belly strips rolled tight with cinnamon-forward Ember rub, smoked, and finished with Ember finishing glaze.
story: Not a dessert — a savory pork belly roll with warm cinnamon spice running through it. Rolled tight, smoked until probe-tender, and lacquered with Ember Finishing Glaze. Serve them on skewers and watch them disappear.

steps.title: Slice
steps.body: Slice the pork belly into long strips, about 1 1/2 inches wide.

steps.title: Rub
steps.body: Coat every strip generously with the cinnamon-esque rub — get it in all the cracks.

steps.title: Roll
steps.body: Roll each strip up tight and tie with twine or skewer through to hold the shape.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 275°F until 200-205°F internal, about 2-3 hours. You want them probe-tender like burnt ends.

steps.title: Glaze
steps.body: Brush with warmed Ember Finishing Glaze during the last 30 minutes. Don't be shy — coat them completely.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Rest 15 minutes. Serve on the skewers with extra glaze for dipping.

proTips: The cinnamon reads as warm spice, not dessert. The cayenne and ginger keep it honest.
Tie them tight or they'll unroll on you.
Cut the twine off before serving unless you want someone flossing with it.

title: Ember Pumpkin Spice Pork Rub
summary: A fall-seasonal Ember rub — warm pumpkin spice built for pork butt, ribs, belly, and loin.
story: Pork and warm spice are old friends — clove-studded ham, apple-cinnamon pork loin. This just puts a name on it. Brown sugar and pumpkin pie spices with enough cayenne to keep the sweet honest. A Halloween-season Ember rub: put it on everything in October and retire it with honor.

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Stir everything together until evenly combined.

steps.title: Use
steps.body: Coat pork butt, ribs, belly, or loin generously. Smoke or grill as usual.

steps.title: Store
steps.body: Keeps in a sealed jar for 6 months — but you won't need it that long in October.

proTips: Don't go heavy-handed past 1/2 tsp on the cloves or it'll taste like a ham from 1974.
Killer on a smoked pork loin with an apple glaze.
Or use your favorite rub — it's not set in stone.

title: Ember Pumpkin Spice BBQ Sauce
summary: A fall BBQ sauce — warm pumpkin spice over a tangy apple-cider base. Built for the pumpkin spice rub.
story: Every great rub deserves a sauce that speaks its language. Apple butter gives this one body and fall-orchard flavor, pumpkin pie spices bring the warmth, and a splash of bourbon keeps it grown-up. Brush it on in the last 15 minutes and let the sugars caramelize. The full October treatment, start to finish.

steps.title: Combine
steps.body: Everything in a saucepan. Stir it smooth.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body: Simmer low for 20 minutes, stirring now and then, until it thickens enough to coat a spoon.

steps.title: Taste
steps.body: Want more tang? Another splash of vinegar. More warm? Another pinch of cinnamon.

steps.title: Jar
steps.body: Cool and jar it. Keeps 3 weeks in the fridge.

proTips: Brush it on ribs or pork loin in the last 15 minutes so the sugars caramelize instead of burn.
Pair it with the Ember Pumpkin Spice Pork Rub for the full October treatment.
Or use your favorite sauce — it's not set in stone.

title: Pumpkin-Spiced Grilled Sweet Potatoes
summary: Sweet potato cubes tossed in Ember pumpkin spice rub, grilled until caramelized and crispy-edged.
story: The side dish that eats like dessert but isn't. Sweet potatoes love warm spice the way pork does — toss them in the Ember pumpkin spice rub with butter and brown sugar, hit them with high heat, and let the edges go crispy and caramelized. They go scary-good next to anything with the pumpkin spice sauce on it.

items: 3 lbs sweet potatoes, peeled and cut into 1-inch cubes
3 Tbsp Ember Pumpkin Spice Pork Rub

steps.title: Toss
steps.body: Toss the cubes with melted butter until every piece is coated.

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Sprinkle the rub, brown sugar, and salt over them. Toss again — get it even.

steps.title: Grill
steps.body: Grill over medium-high heat (about 400°F) in a grill basket or on a sheet pan, 20-25 minutes, turning once. You want crispy caramelized edges. No grill? Roast at 425°F in the oven, same time.

proTips: Cut them even or the small ones burn while the big ones stay hard. One inch, no heroes.
The brown sugar's what gives you those crispy edges — don't skip it.
Or use your favorite rub — it's not set in stone.

title: Venison Pineapple Bratwurst
summary: Sweet pineapple meets savory bratwurst spices in a venison sausage. The Amish know what they're doing.
story: Every year I get a deer, I take it to the Amish and have them turn some of it into pineapple bratwurst. Sweet, savory, juicy — it's the sausage I look forward to all year. This is my version of it: venison and pork butt, crushed pineapple, and classic bratwurst spices, stuffed into hog casings and smoked low.

items: 1 can (20 oz) crushed pineapple, drained well

steps.title: Grind
steps.body: Grind the venison and pork butt together through a coarse plate. Keep everything cold — meat, grinder, all of it.

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Mix in the drained pineapple and all the spices. Add the ice water and mix until it gets sticky and binds together.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.body: Stuff into hog casings, twist into 6-inch links. Don't overstuff or they'll burst.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 180-200°F until they hit 155°F internal, about 2-3 hours. Or grill them over medium heat.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 10 minutes before cutting in.

proTips: Drain that pineapple GOOD. Squeeze it in a towel if you have to. Too much juice and the sausage won't bind.
The pork butt's non-negotiable — straight venison bratwurst comes out dry as a bone.
Or use your favorite sausage seasoning — it's not set in stone.

title: Louisiana Boudin
summary: Cajun rice sausage with pork, liver, and the holy trinity — squeeze it out of the casing like the Cajuns do.
story: Boudin is Louisiana in a casing — pork, liver, rice, and Cajun seasoning, poached and smoked. Don't skip the liver. That's what makes it boudin and not just rice sausage.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body: Simmer pork butt, liver, onion, bell pepper, and garlic in water until tender, about 1.5 hours.

steps.title: Grind
steps.body: Grind through a coarse plate. Mix in the rice, Cajun seasoning, and green onions.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.body: Stuff into hog casings, twist into links.

steps.title: Poach & smoke
steps.body: Poach in simmering water 10 minutes, then smoke at 225°F for 1 hour.

proTips: Don't skip the liver — that's what makes it boudin and not just rice sausage.
Eat it by squeezing it out of the casing like the Cajuns do.
Or use your favorite Cajun seasoning — it's not set in stone.

title: Smoked Andouille
summary: Coarse, peppery, double-smoked Cajun sausage — the one that goes IN the gumbo, not next to it.
story: Andouille is the backbone of Cajun cooking — coarse-ground, heavy on the pepper and garlic, smoked low and slow until it's dark as mahogany. This is the sausage that goes in the gumbo, not next to it.

steps.title: Grind
steps.body: Grind pork and fat coarse. Mix in all spices, curing salt, and ice water until sticky.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.body: Stuff into hog casings, twist into links. Rest overnight in the fridge.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 180°F for 2 hours, then 200°F until 155°F internal, about 4-5 hours total.

proTips: The double smoke is what makes andouille — low and slow, heavy on the pecan or oak.
Use curing salt (Prague Powder #1) since this smokes low for hours — it's a food-safety thing, not optional.
Or use your favorite sausage seasoning — it's not set in stone.

title: Jalapeño Cheddar Venison Sausage
summary: Deer camp classic — venison sausage studded with jalapeños and cheddar, smoked low and slow.
story: Every deer camp needs a jalapeño cheddar sausage. Venison and pork butt, diced jalapeños, and high-temp cheddar, smoked until the casings snap. The heat mellows in the smoke — don't be shy with the peppers.

items: 6 jalapeños, diced (seeds in if you're brave)

steps.title: Grind
steps.body: Grind venison and pork together through a coarse plate. Keep everything cold.

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Mix in jalapeños, cheese, spices, curing salt, and ice water until sticky and bound.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.body: Stuff into hog casings, twist into links.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 180°F for 2 hours, then bump to 200°F until 155°F internal.

proTips: Use high-temp cheese or it'll melt out and leave you with hollow pockets.
The jalapeño heat mellows in the smoke — don't be shy with them.
Or use your favorite sausage seasoning — it's not set in stone.

title: Smoked Breakfast Sausage
summary: Sage-forward breakfast sausage, smoked low — make a big batch and freeze it.
story: The sage is what makes it breakfast sausage — don't skip it. Pork butt and fat, brown sugar, sage, and red pepper flakes, smoked low or fried up in the skillet. These freeze great, so make a big batch and thank yourself later.

steps.title: Grind
steps.body: Grind pork and fat through a coarse plate. Keep everything cold.

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Mix in all spices and ice water until sticky and bound.

steps.title: Form
steps.body: Stuff into casings or form into patties.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 200°F until 155°F internal, about 2 hours. Or just fry the patties.

proTips: The sage is what makes it breakfast sausage — don't skip it.
These freeze great, so make a big batch and thank yourself later.
Or use your favorite breakfast seasoning — it's not set in stone.

title: Venison Snack Sticks
summary: Jerky's easy-eating cousin — smoky venison sticks with a snap. They disappear fast.
story: Venison snack sticks are what jerky wishes it was — same smoky chew, but you can eat them one-handed. Venison and pork, stuffed into collagen casings and smoked low and slow. Low and slow or they'll wrinkle up like raisins. These disappear fast — make double.

steps.title: Grind
steps.body: Grind venison and pork fine. Mix in all spices, curing salt, and ice water until very sticky.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.body: Stuff into collagen casings.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 160°F for 1 hour (no smoke), then 180°F with smoke until 155°F internal, about 4 hours.

steps.title: Chill
steps.body: Ice bath 10 minutes, then hang to dry.

proTips: Low and slow or they'll wrinkle up like raisins.
The ice bath stops the cooking and gives you that snap.
These disappear fast — make double.

title: Real Texas Chili (Chili Con Carne)
summary: No beans. Don't ask. Beef chunks, dried chiles, and time — this is Texas chili the way it's supposed to be.
story: Real Texas chili has no beans — beans are a side dish, not an ingredient. Beef chuck cut into cubes, a puree of toasted dried chiles, cumin, and a long slow simmer until the meat falls apart. Better the next day. Always.

items: 4 lbs beef chuck, cut into 3/4-inch cubes
2 tsp dried oregano (Mexican if you can find it)
Beef tallow or oil for browning

steps.title: Toast & soak
steps.body: Toast the dried chiles in a dry skillet until fragrant, about 2 minutes per side. Soak in hot water 20 minutes, then blend smooth with a little of the soaking liquid.

steps.title: Brown
steps.body: Brown the beef cubes in batches in beef tallow over high heat. Don't crowd the pot. Set aside.

steps.title: Build the base
steps.body: In the same pot, cook the onion until soft. Add garlic, chili powder, cumin, paprika, oregano, salt, and pepper — stir until fragrant, about 1 minute.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body: Pour in the chile puree, beef broth, and beer. Add the beef back in. Simmer low 2.5-3 hours until the beef falls apart.

steps.title: Thicken
steps.body: Stir in masa harina in the last 30 minutes to thicken.

proTips: No beans. This is Texas chili — beans are a side dish, not an ingredient.
Cubes, not ground beef. The texture is the whole point.
The dried chiles are doing the real work here. The chili powder's just backup.
Better the next day. Always.

title: Owensboro Pulled Mutton with Black Dip
summary: Owensboro classic — injected mutton shoulder smoked low, pulled and piled on a bun with tangy black dip.
story: Owensboro, Kentucky has been doing mutton for 150 years, and the black dip is the whole point — tangy, peppery, thin. Not BBQ sauce, don't treat it like one. The shoulder gets injected to stay juicy through the long smoke, then pulled and piled high.

steps.title: Inject
steps.body: Inject the shoulder all over with the broth mixture — get it deep in the thickest parts.

steps.title: Rub & rest
steps.body: Rub all over with salt, pepper, garlic, and paprika. Rest overnight in the fridge.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F over hickory until 200°F internal, 10-12 hours. Mop with black dip every hour after the first 3.

steps.title: Pull
steps.body: Rest 1 hour, pull the meat, and serve piled on a bun with black dip on the side.

proTips: Owensboro's been doing this for 150 years — they know.
The injection keeps it juicy through the long smoke.
The black dip is tangy, peppery, and thin — it's not BBQ sauce, don't treat it like one.

title: Smoked Mutton Ribs
summary: Meaty mutton ribs with a dark bark — treat them like beef ribs, not baby backs.
story: Mutton ribs are meatier than you'd think. Low and slow over hickory, wrapped through the stall, pulled when they probe like butter. These aren't baby backs — give them the full time.

items: Apple juice in a spray bottle

steps.title: Prep
steps.body: Trim the ribs, pull the membrane, rub all over. Rest 1 hour at room temp.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F over hickory, spritzing with apple juice every 45 minutes.

steps.title: Wrap
steps.body: Wrap in butcher paper when they hit the stall (around 160°F). Pull at 200-203°F when they probe tender, 5-6 hours total.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 30 minutes before slicing.

proTips: Mutton ribs are meatier than you'd think — treat them like beef ribs, not baby backs.
They need the full time. Don't rush them.
Or use your favorite rub — it's not set in stone.

title: Grilled Mutton Chops with Mint Chimichurri
summary: Thick mutton chops grilled hot and fast, finished with bright mint chimichurri.
story: Don't overcook mutton chops — medium-rare or don't bother. Thick loin chops, hot grill, a few minutes a side, and a mint chimichurri that cuts the richness perfect.

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Rub chops with olive oil, salt, pepper, and garlic. Rest 1 hour at room temp.

steps.title: Grill
steps.body: Grill hot and fast — 3-4 minutes per side for medium-rare (135°F internal).

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: Blitz the chimichurri ingredients, spoon over the chops, rest 5 minutes.

proTips: Don't overcook mutton chops — medium-rare or don't bother.
The mint chimichurri cuts the richness perfect.
Let them rest — the juices need to settle.

title: Blackened Gator Bites with Remoulade
summary: Gator tail chunks seared black in cast iron, with a cool remoulade for dipping.
story: Gator goes from perfect to rubber in a hurry — hot and fast is the whole trick. Tail meat cut into chunks, coated in blackening seasoning, seared in a screaming-hot skillet, and dunked in homemade remoulade.

items: 2 lbs gator tail meat, cut into 1-inch chunks
3 Tbsp blackening seasoning (or your favorite Cajun seasoning)

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Toss gator chunks in melted butter, then coat heavy with blackening seasoning.

steps.title: Sear
steps.body: Sear in a screaming-hot cast iron skillet, 2-3 minutes per side until blackened and cooked through.

steps.title: Sauce
steps.body: Stir the remoulade ingredients together. Serve the bites hot with remoulade for dipping.

proTips: Don't walk away from the skillet — gator goes from perfect to rubber in a hurry.
Hot and fast is the whole trick.
Or use your favorite Cajun seasoning — it's not set in stone.

title: Gator Sauce Piquante
summary: Cajun gator stew in a dark roux, served over rice — the roux is everything.
story: Sauce piquante is Cajun comfort in a bowl — gator meat simmered in a dark roux with the holy trinity, tomatoes, and stock, served over rice. The roux is everything: dark but not burnt. If it smells scorched, start over. No shame in it.

steps.title: Roux
steps.body: Make a dark roux — oil and flour in a heavy pot, stirring constantly over medium heat until it's the color of peanut butter, 20-30 minutes. Don't burn it.

steps.title: Trinity
steps.body: Add onion, bell pepper, celery, and garlic. Cook until soft.

steps.title: Build
steps.body: Stir in tomatoes, stock, Cajun seasoning, cayenne, and bay leaves. Bring to a simmer.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body: Add gator meat, cover, and simmer 45 minutes to 1 hour until the gator is tender.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Serve over rice with green onions on top.

proTips: The roux is everything — dark but not burnt.
If it smells scorched, start over. No shame in it.
Or use your favorite Cajun seasoning — it's not set in stone.

title: Smoked Lamb Shoulder (Pulled Lamb)
summary: Injected lamb shoulder smoked low until it pulls like pork butt — lamb's lean, the injection keeps it juicy.
story: Lamb's lean like venison, so this shoulder gets injected before it ever sees smoke. Low and slow over oak, wrapped through the stall, pulled at 200°F like a pork butt. The injection is what keeps it from drying out.

steps.title: Inject
steps.body: Inject the shoulder all over, deep into the thickest parts.

steps.title: Rub & rest
steps.body: Rub all over, rest overnight in the fridge.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F over oak until 200°F internal, 8-10 hours. Wrap in butcher paper at the stall.

steps.title: Pull
steps.body: Rest 1 hour, then pull it like pork butt.

proTips: Lamb's lean like venison — the injection is what keeps it from drying out on the long smoke. Don't skip it.
Wrap at the stall to push through faster.
Or use your favorite rub — it's not set in stone.

title: Braised Lamb Shanks
summary: Injected lamb shanks braised in red wine until they fall off the bone, over mashed potatoes.
story: Lamb shanks get the injection treatment too, then a hard sear and a long braise in red wine with rosemary and thyme. They come out falling off the bone over a pile of mashed potatoes, with the sauce doing all the talking.

steps.title: Inject & season
steps.body: Inject the shanks, then season with salt and pepper.

steps.title: Sear

steps.title: Build
steps.body: Cook the veggies in the same pot, add wine and broth, bring to a simmer.

steps.title: Braise

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Serve over mashed potatoes with the braising sauce spooned over.

proTips: The injection plus the braise means these stay juicy all the way through.
Serve over mashed potatoes and let the sauce do the talking.
Skim the fat off the braising liquid before serving if you like.

title: Grilled Lamb Kebabs
summary: Marinated lamb cubes grilled hot and fast with peppers and onions — the marinade does the injection's job.
story: Small cuts can't take an injection, so these kebab cubes go into an olive oil, lemon, garlic, and rosemary marinade overnight. Threaded with peppers and onion, grilled hot and fast to medium-rare. Don't overcook them.

steps.title: Skewer

Soak wooden skewers 30 minutes so they don't burn.

title: Smoked Lamb Ribs with Sticky Glaze
summary: Marinated lamb ribs smoked low with a sticky honey-balsamic glaze brushed on late.
story: Too thin to inject, so these ribs get a garlic-rosemary marinade overnight to stay juicy. Smoked low over oak or cherry, spritzed with apple juice, and finished with a sticky honey-balsamic glaze in the last 30 minutes so it doesn't burn.

steps.title: Smoke

The glaze goes on late so it doesn't burn.

title: Smoked Cornbread Dressing
summary: Day-old cornbread, water chestnuts for crunch, sage and thyme — smoked in cast iron.
story: Day-old cornbread or it falls apart. Onion, celery, water chestnuts for that crunch that survives the whole cook, sage and thyme, packed into a buttered cast iron skillet and smoked until golden. If you made the jalapeño cheddar cornbread, this dressing gets a nice little kick.

items: 1 can (8 oz) water chestnuts, drained and chopped

steps.title: Sauté
steps.body: Sauté onion and celery in butter until soft.

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Mix everything in a big bowl — it should be wet but not soupy.

title: Smoked Turkey Gravy
finish: Thick enough to coat a spoon
summary: Made from smoker drippings with just a whisper of rosemary — liquid gold.
story: Save those drippings from the turkey — that's liquid gold. Put a drip pan under the bird and thank yourself later. Whisked into a gravy with just a little rosemary — pull the sprig before serving so nobody gets a mouthful of needles.

items: Turkey drippings (or 4 Tbsp butter + 4 Tbsp flour if you're short)
1/4 cup flour (if not using drippings roux)

steps.title: Roux
steps.body: If you've got drippings from the smoker, whisk flour into them and cook 2 minutes. If no drippings, make a roux with butter and flour first.

steps.title: Whisk
steps.body: Whisk in broth until thick. Toss in the rosemary sprig.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body: Simmer 10 minutes. Pull the rosemary sprig before serving.

title: Smoked Mashed Potatoes
summary: Potatoes smoked whole in the skin, mashed with butter, cream, and roasted garlic.
story: Smoking the potatoes whole in the skin keeps them from drying out — and you get a whisper of smoke in every bite. Mashed with butter, warm cream, and garlic roasted right on the smoker. The gravy goes on top of these. That's the whole point.

items: 4 cloves garlic, roasted on the smoker

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke the whole potatoes at 275°F for 1.5 hours until tender.

steps.title: Mash
steps.body: Scoop out the insides and mash with butter, sour cream, warm cream, and roasted garlic.

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Salt to taste. Top with chives.

proTips: Smoking them whole in the skin keeps them from drying out.
Warm the cream first — cold cream makes gluey potatoes.
The gravy goes on top of these. That's the whole point.
A little sour cream makes them tangy and rich — Kelly's way.

title: Ember Apple Rub
summary: A sweet Ember rub built on real apple — warm fall spice for pork ribs, shoulder, chops, and chicken.
story: Apple and pork are old friends. This rub puts the orchard right in the jar: freeze-dried apple powder for true apple flavor, brown sugar for the crust, and cinnamon, ginger, and nutmeg for warmth. Use it anywhere you'd reach for a sweet rub — it shines on ribs and pork shoulder.

steps.title: Make the apple powder
steps.body: Buzz a handful of freeze-dried apples in a spice grinder until powder-fine. Measure out 3 tablespoons.

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Combine everything in a bowl and stir until even. Break up any brown sugar lumps with your fingers.

steps.title: Store
steps.body: Keep in a sealed jar. Use within 6 months for best flavor.

proTips.text: Freeze-dried fruit is in the dried-fruit aisle at most grocery stores — no specialty shop needed.

title: Ember Cherry BBQ Sauce
summary: A sweet-tart Ember sauce built on real dark cherries — glossy, rich, and made for pork, chicken, and smoked meatloaf.
story: Cherries and smoke are a natural pair. This sauce cooks fresh or frozen dark cherries down into a ketchup-based BBQ sauce with brown sugar, molasses, and a butter finish. Blend it smooth or leave it a little chunky — either way it shines on ribs and pulled pork.

items: 2 cups fresh or frozen dark sweet cherries, pitted

steps.title: Break down the cherries
steps.body: Simmer the cherries in a saucepan over medium heat until they soften and break down, about 10 minutes. Mash with a spoon.

steps.title: Build the sauce
steps.body: Stir in everything except the butter. Simmer 15–20 minutes, stirring now and then, until thickened.

steps.title: Blend
steps.body: Blend smooth with an immersion blender — or leave it a little chunky if you like texture.

steps.title: Butter finish
steps.body: Stir in the butter off the heat. Cool and jar. Keeps 2 weeks in the fridge.

title: Ember Cranberry BBQ Sauce
summary: A sweet-tart Ember sauce built on real cranberries with orange zest — thin, glossy, and made for the holidays. Turkey's best friend.
story: Cranberries want to be a BBQ sauce — they're already tart, already red, already built for a glaze. This one gets extra brown sugar to tame the tartness, orange zest for brightness, and a butter finish. Thin enough to brush, bold enough to stand up to smoked turkey and pork.

steps.title: Pop the cranberries
steps.body: Simmer the cranberries in a saucepan over medium heat until they pop and break down, about 10 minutes.

steps.title: Build the sauce

steps.title: Blend
steps.body: Blend smooth with an immersion blender — or leave it a little chunky if you like texture.

steps.title: Butter finish
steps.body: Stir in the butter off the heat. Cool and jar. Keeps 2 weeks in the fridge.

title: Ember Dr Pepper BBQ Sauce
summary: A sweet Ember sauce built on reduced Dr Pepper — dark, glossy, and sticky-sweet. Made for ribs, pulled pork, and wings.
story: Dr Pepper's 23 flavors were practically born for BBQ sauce. This one reduces the soda down to concentrate all that cherry-vanilla-spice character, then builds it into a ketchup-based sauce with extra brown sugar and honey for sweetness and a butter finish. Brush it on ribs in the last 30 minutes and watch it turn to candy.

steps.title: Reduce the Dr Pepper
steps.body: Simmer the Dr Pepper in a saucepan until reduced by half, about 15 minutes. This concentrates the flavor.

steps.title: Build the sauce
steps.body: Stir in everything except the butter. Simmer 15–20 minutes, stirring now and then, until thick and glossy.

steps.title: Butter finish
steps.body: Stir in the butter off the heat. Cool and jar. Keeps 2 weeks in the fridge.
